h: A dim green-grey sky, columns of killing gold, and six short hours of night.

Look up during the day and you see no sun. You see the Pale Veil: a vast, faintly luminous overcast of green and grey that covers the sky from coast to coast. It is the body of Sariel, the moon god, spread thin across the heavens. Under it, daylight is gloomy and soft, but safe.

The Veil covers this continent only. Beyond it, at the ragged edges of the map, lie the Fadelands (scholars say Shadelands), where the sun shines unshielded and nothing ordinary survives. Sailors whisper that there may be other protected lands somewhere beyond the sea. Nobody has come back to confirm it.

t: The Wounds and the light columns
h:
The Veil is cracking. Where it splits, the unstable sun pours through in columns of light: pillars of pale gold that stand in the mist like something you could walk into by accident. Some are as thin as a spear, some as wide as a town. They drift slowly with the hours.

Stepping into a column burns you with radiant light, and the burning gets worse the longer you stay. The light does not only burn: it distorts. It is the light that killed the Tree of Life.

And there is worse. Anyone who dies in the light is erased from history. Their name fades from records, their face from memory, their place from every story. A mother forgets she had a son. A town forgets it had a mayor. People only notice the gaps: an empty chair, a name scratched out in a ledger, a bead missing from a braid.

"Walk in the grey. Never in the gold."
— first thing every child is taught

The world still turns, but strangely: it is only truly dark from about 9 in the evening to 3 in the morning. Eighteen hours of gloomy day, six hours of precious night. Night is when people feel safest, gather, pray and tell stories. Dawn, at the end of the dark, is when runes are re-marked for the day ahead.

The cracks grow slowly. Scholars agree the Veil will last thousands of years more, but every generation the safe land gets a little smaller, and the light columns a little more common. Many are searching for a way to mend the Veil. None has found it.

The Chronicle calls this time the threshold between the Third and Fourth Ages. By old custom, a new age can only be named when the world takes a turn for the better. If this is rock bottom, no one can say.

Beneath your feet lies the abandoned world of the dwarves: tunnels, rail lines and buried cities, all collapsed and sealed with great gates. From down there rose the Mana Plagues. Going down is forbidden, in many places a heresy. The rust-red lines that still cross the land are the old dwarven rails, leading to tunnel mouths that no longer open.
As the monasteries and the Chronicle tell it. Each age lasts roughly a thousand years and ends with a great event.

t: The First Age: the Descent of Form
h:
The angels came down and gave the formless world its shape, each one embodying a principle: memory, silence, flesh, motion. From their work rose the Emanations, which common folk call the Vast. They were not giants or gods. They were shapes too big and too strange to understand, with no faces, no voices and no minds like ours. They held reality in place. The first mortal peoples took shape in their shadow, and nobody knows if that was meant or an accident.

Then came the Fracture of Names. The angels' domains overlapped and turned on each other. The Vast faltered: some broke apart and tore the land as they fell, others went still and hardened into the mountains and continents you walk on today. In the Dissolution, the angels were unmade, and their essence bled into the leylines, the storms, strange relics, and the blood and bone of every living thing.

Scholars name the Emanations with the old words of the Tree: Keter, Chesed, Gevurah, Yesod, Malkuth and others. Nobody knows if they thought, felt, or even noticed us. No two old pictures of one agree. All are gone now, and which mountain was which is lost to time, with one exception: the one the southern people call Odilon. (Older texts call them Titans.)

t: The War of Shade and Sun
h:
At the turn of the age, the gods of the sun and sky ruled the heavens. The surface peoples, above all the elves and the dwarves, banded together and rose against them. A few tried to defend the gods; they failed. The sun and sky gods died.

The victory was a disaster. Without its gods, the sun turned unstable, and its light began to kill.

To save the world, the moon god Sariel, Angel of the Waning Moon, gave himself up. His body was poured across the sky and became the Pale Veil. Sariel is dead, but scattered pieces of him remain in the world, and they still hold power.
k: Sariel, Angel of the Waning Moon

t: The Second Age: the Age of Iron Psalms
h:
The dwarves delved deeper than any people before or since. They found that the divine residue left by the angels could be harnessed, and they built an empire on it: soul-furnaces, memory-engines, flesh-forges, railways spanning the continent, iron cities whose furnaces never dimmed. They quarried the remains of the Vast.

The surface peoples, the dwarves' old allies against the gods, saw it as desecration. The Severance Wars followed, fought with weapons that tore reality and burned the sky.

At the end of the age, the dwarves tried to build an angel. They nearly succeeded. What they made was incomplete, and its waking caused the Silence of Heaven: magic collapsed, whole regions were erased, and the dwarven empire fell within a generation.

t: The Third Age: the Age of Ashen Reclamation
h:
From the deepest tunnels came the Mana Plagues: stone that pulsed like flesh, caverns that breathed, creatures that were only half a shape, voices with no mouth. They spread upward. So the peoples abandoned the deep. The great arcane orders and the last dwarven engineers collapsed the Deep Roads and sealed them with gates of stone, sigil and spell. Some routes were erased from every map.

The surface was rebuilt around quiet places and stable leylines. Descent became taboo under the Doctrine of Ascent. True enchantment was lost; alchemy and runes took its place.

About seventy years ago, a vast deposit of Devinum crystal was found at Skinter Spire on the Palcox plateau. Every power raced to mine it. So much Devinum was used that the Veil split over the main mining town. Everyone there died and was erased: today it is the Unnamed Town, empty houses and ledgers full of blank names. The same night an old Deep Road gate nearby began to sing and failed. The plague got out. The plateau was burned and closed. Old people still call that night the Gate that Sang.
The end of the Third Age. The seals hold, mostly. Some gates have begun to hum. The safe land shrinks. And everyone is waiting to see whether anything will ever get better.
The gods are dead or silent. Faith goes on anyway.

The gods are very absent. Nobody you know has heard one answer. The angels who survived the ages are distant, and can be reached only in very special circumstances.

Clerics are rare: perhaps three hundred on the whole continent can truly work miracles. They do not draw on a god but on the domains the angels hold: death, dreams, judgement, mercy and the like. A real cleric is a figure of awe, and often of envy.

Paladins need no god at all. Their power comes from their oath. Keep it, and it holds you up. Break it, and it breaks you.

The greatest faith on the continent worships the dead moon god. Sariel died for the world and his body still shields it, so his cult is everywhere: shrines in every town, pilgrims, preachers, processions at night. It is vast, rich, and fierce, and it treats doubt about Sariel as treason against the living. His sacrifice holds the world together, and the cult means to make sure nobody forgets it.

The cult prizes the scattered pieces of Sariel above all things.

In the south, people honour Odilon, the one Emanation whose name was never forgotten. When the Vast fell, Odilon did not tear the land. It went still, and two lakes welled up out of it: Odilon's Tears. Whatever drinks their water grows, which is why the south stays green. Southerners say Odilon wept for us. Scholars say nobody can know what an Emanation feels, or if it feels at all. People do not pray to Odilon. They leave small offerings at the water and whisper thank you.

Scholars of the Tree say Odilon is the Emanation called Chesed, Mercy, though the name is ours, not its. Most southerners have never heard the word.

When you die, Azrael, the gatherer, comes for your soul and takes it to Varjohalli, the Unlit Hall: an endless, gentle shade where the dead finally rest from the sun. Funerals are held at night, and the dead are wrapped in dark cloth so the light cannot find them. Families keep the names of their dead in a house book, because a soul nobody remembers is said to wander. Old folk say there are more ghosts than there used to be.

The erased do not go to Varjohalli. Nobody knows where they go. That is the true horror of the light.

A heresy is spreading: the Unveiled believe that the sun gods will return if the Veil falls, that the distorting light is a rebirth, and that being erased is a kind of freedom. The Cult of Sariel hunts them.

Scholars and priests still keep the old names. What follows is what people believe, not what is known. For more about each being, see angelarium.net.

Clerics: talk to your DM about which angel's domain you draw on.

ch: The Lands and Who Rules Them
t: The Lands and Who Rules Them
h:
No empire, no high king. A dozen powers that need each other and trust nobody.

Power is split between many, held in an uneasy coexistence. Every power has a role to fill, even the ones everyone dislikes. A world this small and fragile cannot afford open war, so conflict happens in shadows, trade deals and marriages.

ch: The Lands and Who Rules Them
h:
The great lake-city on the east shore of Mooneye Lake is ruled by the Dusk Court, five vampires. Most have held it for longer than anyone can remember:

  • Lord Aurelian Vesk
  • Lady Isolde Karmine
  • Hrafn Ulvedal
  • Old Nachtmar
  • Lady Asagiri

Asper is where north and south meet, and where Pohjal and Minago blend into a trade pidgin. It is rich and very strictly ordered. See The Six Great Cities below.

ch: The Lands and Who Rules Them
h: The great lake in the heart of the continent. At night it seems to hold a moon, though there is none in the sky: a soft glow far below the islands of Kirous Vesi, "cursed water". Fishermen do not sail near the islands.

ch: The Lands and Who Rules Them
h: The wood-elf city at the edge of Eternal Darkness is governed by twin Stewards, Lehtiär and Lumiär, Leaf and Snow, who always rule together and never appear apart.

ch: The Lands and Who Rules Them
h: A forest so deep that the light never reaches the floor, a refuge in daylight. Somewhere inside stands the Red Chapel, where the Veilsworn knights swear their vows in blood.

ch: The Lands and Who Rules Them
h: Once a Viking-style hold in the snowy north beneath Korven Lihd, Linnoitus threw out its jarls. It is now run by the Hearthmoot, a council of its human workers, led by Speaker Sigrun Halla. Everything is shared, everyone works, and outsiders find it either inspiring or terrifying.

ch: The Lands and Who Rules Them
h: The north-eastern fortress is the seat of House Kettilgrund, a dwarven merchant house that trades across the continent. Dwarves are frowned upon, but nobody refuses Kettilgrund silver.

ch: The Lands and Who Rules Them
h: In the northern mountains, above a valley glittering with purple crystal, rules the drow matriarchy of Matron Velisra. The drow sell their crystal a little at a time, and nobody asks them too many questions.

ch: The Lands and Who Rules Them
h: In the far north lies the carcass of a huge aboleth, dead for ages, sprawled across one of the old Deep Road gates. The Lukkar guard it closely.

ch: The Lands and Who Rules Them
h: The green south is a land of mossy cedar forests, shrines and spirits in the trees, where people speak Minago. Its fey elves are ruled from Kaigan by Oboro, the Hazy King, named for the moon seen through mist.

ch: The Lands and Who Rules Them
h: The red west is a forest of giant red mushrooms whose caps shade the ground like a living Veil. It belongs to Nilith, the Toadstool Queen, a fey ruler and the Hazy King's oldest rival. Their feud is older than most cities.

ch: The Lands and Who Rules Them
t: Skinter Spire and the Palcox Plateau
h: The south-east, scarred by the Glass Rush. Purple crystal, burned ground, the Unnamed Town, and a gate nobody goes near.

ch: The Lands and Who Rules Them
h:
At the northern and south-eastern edges, the clouds of the Veil thin and tear. Beyond lies the unprotected world. Strange creatures live there, newcomers or things changed by the light. Taivari clans walk its borders; few others dare.

The Fadelands also wear things away: colours, memories, even people. Travellers who stay too long start to drift and forget. Experienced guides never cross without Brill (see chapter 10).
What any traveller could tell you. The rest you find out for yourself.

Canals, boats and bridges on the shore of Mooneye Lake. Light columns fall only far out on the water, and boatmen know how to steer around them. The Dusk Court rules, and the people revere them: the lands around Asper are full of monsters, and the Court keeps them out.

Asper sells everything: relics and salvage nobody else can get, the goods of north and south, and lake pearls and moon-water. The law is very strict, and needless bloodshed is punished severely. Look for the Drowned Cathedral and the Bridge of Lanterns, one lantern for every citizen.

A column of light, the Hearthfire, burns in the middle of the city, and Linnoitus is built in rings around it: forge-halls at the edge of the light, old Viking longhouses, then the crews' halls. Every street points to the light. Walk toward it, never into it.

It is famous for Hearthfire steel and sunglass, which glows faintly forever. Burn scars are badges of honour, and in the Hearthmoot work earns voice. Children learn the Three Great Wrongs: hoarding, shirking a shift, and feeding someone to the light. The Shift Bell rules the day.

A city inside a vast old dwarven station hall, where the rails come up out of the ground. Platforms are market streets and dead carriages are shops. The one place dwarves are on top. Stationmaster Hallvard Kettilgrund has the final word.

Westermark lives on salvage, the scrap of a dead empire. Opening a tunnel is punished by death. Everyone visits the Last Engine, frozen at the end of Platform One.

Living trees grown together into one great dome, with the city among the roots below, lit by glowing moss. The twin Stewards Lehtiär and Lumiär speak as one, beside an empty throne no one may touch.

Fylson sells living wood, healing herbs and shade-trees that can shelter a whole town, and every ruler wants one. Strangers trade at the forest's edge and are watched under the dome. Destroying a record or a name is the worst crime. The elves keep every name in the Hall of Songs.

A drow city hanging under a cliff that curls over like a stone wave, lit from below by the purple crystal fields of Calathgar. Matron Velisra, priestess of Bezaliel, Angel of Shadows, rules from the castle on the crest. Others live lower down and work the fields for shelter.

The drow sell crystal a little at a time, and quieter goods to those who ask. Crystal thieves are thrown from the Fall. Mind your step on the Silk Bridge.

A colossal stone pillar above the southern cedar forests, hollowed into terraces inside and hung with shrines and red bridges outside. Sometimes a cloud drifts in and the city disappears. Oboro, the Hazy King, rules over a fey Court of Seasons.

Kaigan trades tear-water that heals, and deals in favours and dreams. Use a courtesy name, never a true one, and leave cold iron at the door. See the Hollow and the Season Gardens.

The classic peoples are everywhere. A few are not like anywhere else.

Humans, elves, dwarves, halflings, gnomes, orcs and the other familiar peoples of the 2024 Player's Handbook are common across the continent. Tieflings, aasimar, goliaths and similar peoples exist but are rare outliers, and are stared at wherever they go.

The north speaks Pohjal, a hard, clipped tongue, from Linnoitus and Korven Lihd down to Fylson and Westermark. Its names sound Nordic and Finnish.

The south speaks Minago, soft and flowing, through Odilon, Kaigan and Nishikaigan. Its names sound Japanese.

Around Asper the two blend into a market pidgin. Peoples also keep their own tongues (Elvish, Dwarvish and so on).

PeopleWhere and how
HumansEverywhere; Linnoitus is theirs. Most of the Hearthmoot, the Cult of Sariel and the Veilsworn.
Wood elvesFylson and Eternal Darkness. Remember the War of Shade and Sun as their ancestors' great deed.
Fey elvesKaigan and Odilon under the Hazy King; the mushroom courts of Nilith.
DrowCastle Brennenberg and Calathgar Valley. Secretive.
DwarvesScattered among other peoples, or roaming the old dwarven mountains. Westermark's House Kettilgrund. Many Lukkar engineers.
Halflings, gnomesMarket towns, alchemists' guilds, rune-wright workshops.
TaivariThe open plains and the edges of the light. See chapter 6.
FadebornAnywhere, usually on the margins. See chapter 7.
Rare peoplesAsper, where the Dusk Court asks few questions, and the road.

Dwarves helped kill the sun gods, built and broke the greatest empire in history, and caused the Silence of Heaven. Many blame them for the Mana Plagues too. They live among everyone else, but they are frowned upon: served last, watched closely, blamed first. Some dwarves accept it as a debt; others are tired of paying.

Thanks to the Dusk Court, vampires are a known part of the world rather than a myth. Most people fear them; Asper's people mostly pay their taxes and keep their doors shut at night.

A Taivari wanderer on the open plains, a light column behind

Sun-hardened wanderers of the open plains. ( Taival is Pohjal for "the long road".)

Broad and heavy-shouldered, with tusked jaws and thick grey to slate-blue skin that hangs in heavy, leathery folds at the neck, brow and shoulders (the folds shade them from the light), some with curling ram horns, the Taivari look like the warriors of old songs. They are nothing of the kind. The Taivari are a peaceful, nomadic people who have never raised a banner against anyone.

Their gift is the sun. No other people stand the light as well as they do. So their clans walk the open plains that others fear, following old routes from shade-grove to shade-grove along the edges of the light columns. Settled folk need them: Taivari caravans carry silver, salt and news, guide travellers past the columns, and bring back the dying before the light takes them. They are welcome everywhere and belong nowhere.

The Braid of Roads

A Taivari adds one bead, ring or charm to their braids for every journey survived. An elder's hair is a life's map, heavy with old gold, perhaps the last gold still moving freely in the world.

Guest-Right

Anyone who shares shade with a Taivari camp is safe there until dawn, whoever they are. Breaking guest-right is the one thing a clan never forgives.

Names. A clan name and a road name earned on a first journey. Given: Abru, Dhoma, Grell, Haska, Ivruk, Maudra, Oghran, Sefa, Thurra, Ulmo. Road names: Long-Stride, Shade-Finder, Saltbearer, Ninth Bead, Walks-at-Noon. Clans: the Ashmoor, the Hollowcairn, the Tenwinds, the Redgrass.

In the world. Fadeborn often fall in with Taivari caravans; both know the edge of the light, and nobody in camp asks where they came from. Dwarves get the same guest-right as anyone. Many Veilsworn are Taivari. Some clans walk right to the Fadelands' border and scavenge Devinum there.

Creature Type
Humanoid
Size
Medium (about 6½–7½ feet tall)
Speed
35 feet

As a Taivari, you have these special traits.

Sun-Hardened. You have Resistance to Radiant damage. When you enter a light column or start your turn in one, you can ignore its damage for that turn. You can do this a number of times equal to your Proficiency Bonus, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a Long Rest.
Powerful Build. You have Advantage on any ability check you make to end the Grappled condition. You also count as one size larger when determining your carrying capacity.
Plainswalker. When you travel at a Normal or Fast pace, you and up to six companions can't become lost by nonmagical means, and difficult terrain from natural ground doesn't slow your group's travel pace.
Road-Beads. When you fail an ability check or a saving throw, you can touch the beads in your braids and add 1d4 to the roll, possibly turning it into a success. You can use this trait a number of times equal to your Proficiency Bonus, and you regain all expended uses when you finish a Long Rest.
A Fadeborn at the edge of the Fadelands

The faceless ones who walk out of the Fadelands.

Every so often, someone walks out of the Fadelands. Alone or in small groups, they cross the burning edge and come into the shade of the Veil. They have no memory of the journey, and nobody knows where they started. These are the Fadeborn.

A Fadeborn's face is entirely smooth: a pale grey surface with nothing on it but a small mouth. They have no eyes and no ears. They are the tallest of the common peoples, with arms longer than any other. Their pale, light-repelling skin is why they survive the Fadelands, and it makes them hard for the light to hurt.

Fadeborn seem unable to have children. Every one ever seen came out of the Fadelands. Nothing more is known for certain.

Without eyes or ears, Fadeborn sense the world through a kind of mind-sonar. They say it gives them colour, sound and even smell, like anyone else. Other people find it unsettling that a Fadeborn sees the world as a picture inside its own head.

Most of the time a Fadeborn's skin is plain light grey. But they can make faintly glowing coloured patterns appear on their bodies. With no face to show feelings, these patterns and colours are how they show what they feel. People who live with Fadeborn learn to read them.

No Fadeborn remembers its homeland clearly. Yet most faintly remember white, dome-like buildings. Fadeborn use the white dome in their art and crafts, and many carry one or two white round objects that stir that lost memory.

Fadeborn do not build towns of their own. They join whatever people they meet first and learn their ways. One who meets fishermen becomes a fisher; one who meets a Taivari caravan walks the plains. They learn fast, and they copy others disturbingly well.

How people treat them depends on who you ask. Some believe they are made by strange magic as part of some plan. Some fear them, some pity them, some shun them. Some in the Cult of Sariel revere them as people who walked out of the light unharmed. Those without prejudice find them as capable of good or evil as anyone else.

Naming

Fadeborn arrive without names. Most take one from the people who take them in, so a Fadeborn raised by northern miners has a Pohjal name and one raised by southern fishers a Minago one. Others are named for what they are: Dome, Pale, Quiet, Long-Arm, Tallow.

Creature Type
Humanoid
Size
Medium (about 6½ to 7½ feet tall)
Speed
30 feet

As a Fadeborn, you have these special traits.

Inner Eye. You sense the world with your mind instead of eyes and ears. You have Darkvision with a range of 60 feet. You have Advantage on saving throws you make to avoid or end the Blinded or Deafened condition.
Light-Repelling Skin. You have Resistance to Radiant damage.
Long Reach. When you make a melee attack on your turn, your reach for it is 5 feet greater than normal.
Mimic. When you finish a Long Rest, you gain proficiency in one skill of your choice, copied from someone you spent time with. It lasts until you finish your next Long Rest.
Glowing Patterns. As a Bonus Action, you can make your patterns glow, shedding Dim Light in a 10-foot radius, or make them stop. People who know Fadeborn well can read your mood from the colours.
What everyone knows, and what everyone says.
The largest faith on the continent, honouring the god who died to make the Veil. Present everywhere, rich, zealous. Good friends, terrible enemies. Seeks the scattered pieces of Sariel.

Valankantajat in Pohjal, "oath-bearers". An order of oath-knights who stand between the living and the light. They guard the edges of the light columns, escort caravans past them, and drag the dying out of the gold before they can be erased. Each knight swears a personal vow at the Red Chapel in Eternal Darkness, and the vow is the source of their power. A knight who breaks their vow loses it and is called Cracked.

The Cult of Sariel claims the Veilsworn as its holy warriors. The Veilsworn politely refuse to kneel to anyone, which the cult has never forgiven.

t: The Lukkar, Keepers of the Lock
h:
The order of mages and dwarven engineers who sealed the Deep Roads at the end of the Second Age, and still guard the gates. They maintain the seals, the magic-dampening fields and the memory-scrambling sigils, and they hunt anyone who tries to go down. Their ranks are Keyholders (gate commanders), Sigilwrights (seal-keepers) and Silent Wardens, who had their own memories of the tunnels wiped so they could never betray them.

The Lukkar are too few and short of money, and many still blame them for the Gate that Sang.

A rumour, mostly. A secret society of scholars and dwarven exiles who believe they can push the world across the threshold into a Fourth Age by fixing the Veil. They are said to delve illegally into the deep for lost dwarven knowledge, and to be funded by someone rich. Whispers point at House Kettilgrund.
Heretic sun-worshippers who think the old gods will return if the Veil falls, and that erasure is freedom. Hunted by the cult, the Veilsworn and nearly everyone else.
Every city has them, and every guild has a tunnel somewhere that leads further down than it should. Smuggling Devinum, relics and forbidden dwarven salvage pays very well.
The respectable face of magic. They regulate potions, salves and elixirs, and their seals are trusted where enchanters are not.
Carvers who mark runes for a fee. Every town has at least one. They work at dawn.

Every class works. Some are rarer, stranger or more watched than usual.

ClassWhere it fits
ArtificerRune-wrights, alchemists and salvagers of dwarven ruins. Carefully licensed; their work is close to the lost art of enchantment.
BarbarianNorthern Pohjal clans of Korven Lihd; Taivari who channel the sun; survivors of the Fadelands' edge.
BardKeepers of the Chronicle, cult chanters, Asper's court entertainers, and those who memorise the names of the erased so somebody remembers.
ClericVery rare (about 300 on the continent). Draws on an angel's domain, not a god. Expect awe, envy, and constant requests for help. Talk to your DM first.
DruidOdilon's shrine-keepers, Nilith's mushroom circles, Fylson's forest wardens.
FighterCaravan guards, city watch, Lukkar gate soldiers, Dusk Court enforcers.
MonkThe monasteries that copy the Chronicle; southern shrine orders; night-walkers who train in the six dark hours.
PaladinPowered by oath, not god. The Veilsworn are the great order, but any sworn vow can make a paladin.
RangerLight-column guides, Fadelands scouts, Taivari pathfinders.
RogueThieves' guilds, Devinum smugglers, illegal delvers, Kynnys agents.
SorcererThe angels' essence bled into the blood of living things. Sorcerers carry more of it than most, sometimes a trace of Devinum itself. Some are feared as plague-touched.
WarlockPacts with surviving angels, with a piece of Sariel, with something in the sealed deep, or with a member of the Dusk Court.
WizardThe Lukkar, the arcane orders, scholars of the Chronicle. Wizards study magic's remnants carefully, at cost.

Laserllama's alternate and new classes (Magus, Psion, Savant, Shaman, Vessel, Warlord and others) are welcome. Ask your DM about their runes and relics.
"We no longer command magic. We negotiate with its remnants, carefully, and at cost."

Devinum is what the gods were made of. In the world it appears as crystal, often purple, sometimes glowing faintly. It is the most valuable substance on the continent and the most dangerous.

  • It is a source of enormous magical power.
  • Using large amounts of it cracks the Veil. The Glass Rush proved that.
  • It is said to be the only thing that could mend the Veil, if anyone knew how.
  • Most of it is held by the ruling families. The rest lies in the sealed deep or in the Fadelands, so anyone else who wants it must go somewhere forbidden or lethal.
  • A rumour says clean Devinum can cure the Mana Plague.

Brill is a pale, silvery metal found only where the Fadelands blur into nothing. It is light, very strong and oddly hard to see: its shine dims if you look straight at it, and miners say you find it more by feel than by sight. Brill doesn't fade, and it shields whoever carries it from the fading of the Fadelands.

  • Brill cloaks, woven from hair-thin threads, shimmer like frost in moonlight. They are the best-known protection in the Fadelands. They are expensive, slow to make and handed down in families.
  • Brill amulets and rings are said to guard a sleeper's dreams or anchor a person's sense of self.

Rumours: unworked Brill slowly fades away. A Brill cloak remembers everyone who has worn it.

Enchanted objects are seen as vessels of unstable divine residue. Many believe they cause corruption of mind or body, or plague-like symptoms. Powerful relics are hidden, regulated, or outright banned in many cities. Markets exist, but they move, and they are protected by people who don't mind risk.

To a common citizen, a magic item is not a prize. It is a liability. Walking into a town with a glowing sword is asking for trouble.
Items from earlier ages, made with arts now lost, are called Divergent Epoch relics. Most are old rune relics. They are rare, coveted and feared.

Where enchantment is distrusted, alchemy is trusted: measurable, repeatable, controllable. Potions, salves and elixirs are sold openly, under guild seal. A Potion of Healing is ordinary; a magic ring is not.
No living crafter can bind lasting magic into an object. Nobody agrees whether the Silence of Heaven destroyed the art or whether the knowledge simply died. What survives is rune magic.
Runes are not enchantments. They are interfaces: marks that channel the residue already around you.

Weapons, armour and tools are commonly made with empty slots: a flat on the blade, a boss on the shield, a plate inside the helm, a margin in a spellbook. A rune is carved, inked or branded into a slot, or onto the skin. Runes can be added, changed or removed; their effects are limited but predictable.

• Slots, not limits. There is no limit on how many runes you can bear: your gear decides. Each rune needs its own empty slot. A common item has 1 slot, a well-made one 2, and a masterwork or old dwarven piece up to 3. Your skin counts as one extra slot. Runes need no attunement.
  • Who can use a rune. A rune works for anyone who bears it, unless it names a class feature (Rage, Wild Shape, Hex and so on): then only that class can use it.
  • Carving. Carving a new rune takes 1 hour during a rest and needs Calligrapher's Supplies or proficiency in Arcana, or a rune-wright's fee of 50 silver.
  • Re-marking at dawn. Runes fade. Each rune must be re-marked at dawn (about 3 in the morning, as the night ends) to work for the coming day: a few minutes per rune, retracing it with ink, ash, blood or a blade. A rune that isn't re-marked goes dark until the next dawn.
  • Recharge. Any rune or relic with limited uses regains them at dawn.
  • Wear. Runes degrade with use and must eventually be recarved. Your DM may call for a recarving after a hard adventure, a critical failure, or exposure to the plague.
Rune upkeep is a daily ritual. Every camp at dawn is quiet but for the scratch of styluses.
Dawn is the end of the short night, when the Veil turns from black to grey. Rune-wrights say the residue in the world is calmest then, settled by the dark, and that a mark made at dawn holds all day.

With so few clerics, every class must keep itself alive. These rules are always in play.

Moonmarrow

Everyone born under the Veil carries a sliver of the slain moon in the bone. While you are Bloodied, on a turn when you drop a foe, you can spend one Hit Point Die as a Reaction and regain HP (roll + Con). Once per Short Rest.

Shade-Rest

Rest in true shade (stone, deep wood, night) and reroll 1s on Hit Dice. Any Long Rest away from a hearth restores only half your Hit Dice. In the open Fadelands, a Short Rest restores no Hit Dice at all.

Ashmoss Poultice

A mundane remedy (5 silver). Someone with Medicine proficiency can apply it as a Utilize action: the treated creature spends one Hit Point Die outside a rest. Once per creature per Short Rest.

• Potions are a Bonus Action to drink (2024 rules). Alchemists sell them openly.
  • Hit Point Dice on a Short Rest are your real healing budget.
  • Durable, Healer, Chef, Tough and Inspiring Leader are strong feat picks here.

Silver is the standard. Prices, wages and taxes are counted in silver by weight. Gold is rare: the deep veins are sealed, so gold is hoarded by crowns, temples and old houses, and seldom seen in a market. Copper is for village barter.

A medieval world living among the ruins of a lost industry. No working dwarven machines, no gunpowder, no clockwork. The old rails are rust; the engines are dead.

Roads bend around the light columns. Caravans hire Taivari guides or Veilsworn escorts. Travel by day is normal under the Veil; the danger is straying into the gold. Night travel is common, for comfort rather than safety.

Everyone knows the signs:

  1. The Echo. You hear voices that aren't there, and small memories slip away.
  2. The Glassing. Dark crystal veins grow under the skin, and magic misfires near you.
  3. The Unmaking. The body loses its shape, and you forget your own name, becoming one of the half-formed things from below.

Alchemists can slow the first two stages, and the crystal can be cut out, painfully. The third stage cannot be undone. Plague comes from the deep, from cursed relics, and from breaches near the old gates.
Under the Doctrine of Ascent, descending into the deep is taboo and in many places heresy. The Lukkar arrest delvers on sight.

• "Walk in the grey." (Be careful.)
  • "Gone to gold." (Erased; spoken softly, about someone you can't quite remember.)
  • "Mark it at dawn." (Do the boring work so the day goes right.)
  • "Dwarf-luck." (Building something great that ruins everything.)
  • "Not yet the Fourth." (Things are bad, but not hopeless.)
How people count their days, and the nights they keep.

Years are counted AV, After the Veil, from Sariel's Sacrifice. It is now about 2,000 AV.

The Cult named the months after the ten Seraphim. A year has ten months of 36 days. After the last month come the five Veiled Days, which belong to no month. On those days nobody works, marries or signs a contract.

Firstlight (1 Sandalphon). New Year. At the first dawn everyone has their runes re-carved fresh, and children are given their first rune slot, a small iron ring or bead. Rune-wrights work for three days without sleep.

Thread Day (12 Suchlaph). A grey thread is tied in the window "to help hold up the sky", one for each person you love. Touching the Veil-weavers' great grey banner brings luck. A house with no threads is a house with no one left.

The Burning Week (1–7 Uriel). The light is at its brightest, so the cities sleep by day and live by night. The Night Markets are the biggest of the year, and Taivari guides charge triple.

Lantern Night (Asper, 20 Sahaqiel). Thousands of candle-boats drift across the lake for the dead. The Dusk Court stands on the Bridge of Lanterns, and on this one night any citizen may speak to them.

Cold Forge (Linnoitus, 1 Ananiel). For one day the forges go dark. The Shift Bell rings once and the Hearthmoot votes. At dusk, masked smiths compete in the Stand: who dares work closest to the Hearthfire.

Engine Day (Westermark, 15 Remiel). The great salvage fair. Offerings are left on the Last Engine, and hand-carts race down the old rails. The winner rides the Engine's footplate for an hour.

The Night of Debts (last night of Simikiel). Every debt is paid or forgiven before midnight, or it follows you into the dark. Duels are legal in most cities until dawn.

The Naming (30 Azrael). Families read the names of their dead aloud from the house book, and temples read the city's list until dawn. Forgetting a name brings bad luck.

Silk Night (Brennenberg, 18 Shateiel). The silk bridges are strung with glowing crystal, and the drow dance beneath the overhang. For this one night the valley workers may cross the Silk Bridge into the upper city.

Waiting Night (Fylson, 1 Leliel). The Hall of Songs sings the elves' whole history from dusk to dawn. A feast is laid before the empty throne, and every home leaves one seat empty.

Mistfall (Kaigan, no fixed day). When a cloud swallows the pillar, the bells ring, everyone masks, and the dream-market opens. No true name is spoken while the mist lasts, whether that is an hour or a week.

Road's End (the Veiled Days). The Taivari caravans meet in one great camp. Each traveller adds a road-bead for the year, and the elders read the braids aloud. It is the best place to hire a guide or hear news.

The Waning Night (last Veiled Day). The anniversary of Sariel's Sacrifice and the Cult's holiest night. Every flame is put out, and people keep vigil in total darkness until dawn. Whoever lights a fire is shunned for a year.
